rv.q: The fragments augment, rather than interrupt.
In London as in Manchester, this bizarre, inspired hybrid artwork strikes me as exactly the sort of thing the RSC should be doing alongside its more traditional core work.
The show is an inky black, nightmarish jumble of the play’s key scenes that wilfully trades off a certain degree of coherency but none of the intensity.
Her shiver-inducing rendition of Sail to the Moon is the show’s unarguable highlight, a moment of pure, piercing emotion that stands out among the frantic visuals and doomy music.
Whatever it is, though, it’s neat to look at and listen to but far too rushed to triumph.
It’s an electrifying night at the theatre which will live long in the memories of every audience member.

What does remain has been skilfully filleted by Jones and Hoggett - whose other collaborations (as designer and choreographer) include Harry Potter and the Cursed Child - to tell the story lucidly and with real dramatic momentum.
The result is bleak yet stylish, rushed but engaging, slick and yet a Hamlet-by-numbers with a nod to the age of vastly diminished attention spans and quick fixes.
Ultimately, Hamlet Hail to the Thief sacrifices philosophical depth for visceral sensory punch.
The cuts – the play is down from around three hours to an unbroken 100 minutes – strip out most of the poetry, and all the thought.
One of the most gripping, frenetic and visceral productions this reviewer has ever seen.
Hamlet Hail to the Thief barely lets you catch your breath, whilst looking and sounding incredible.
This is an exhilarating piece of theatre and proof that a risk can often pay off, especially when the source material, no matter how disparate, is placed in the right hands.
Endlessly moving, musically arresting and effortlessly personal, this production proves that sometimes the most contrasting things create the perfect match.
This is an innovative take on the text and a stunning production which will prove most effective to Radiohead fans.

Radiohead are a useful sauce to disguise something “good for the child,” the adaptation a decent gateway into Shakespeare, but no more than a chaotic experiment for those familiar with the Bard, alas.
A thundering whirlwind of a production that jolts us to the core.
Far from being just a contemporary reinterpretation, this is a production that packs a punch, sending shivers through the audience with the force of its layered staging.
However, while there were very many elements of this work we enjoyed, we didn't feel it came together as a particular coherent whole.

cn.t: This stylish fusion of Shakespeare and Radiohead's music divides critics: most praise its atmospheric visuals and live band, but some find it emotionally cold. The radical cuts to Hamlet's text prove polarizing.
